Avodah Zarah 67b:7.english: And the opinion of the other tanna, Rabbi Shimon, who deems the mixture permitted if the flavor imparted is detrimental, can be explained in accordance with the opinion of Rav Huna, son of Rav Ḥiyya; as Rav Huna, son of Rav Ḥiyya, says: With regard to the vessels of gentiles, the Torah prohibits only a bat yoma pot (a pot that was used for cooking on that very day), which does not yet impart flavor to the detriment of the food cooked in it. Rather, the flavor that it imparts is not considered detrimental. And the opinion of the other tanna, Rabbi Meir, can also be explained in accordance with this statement, as in his opinion, even in the case of a bat yoma pot, it is not possible that it does not detract from the flavor of food that is subsequently cooked in it even slightly.

Avodah Zarah 67b:8.hebrew: ור"ש מאי טעמא דתניא (דברים יד, כא) לא תאכלו כל נבלה לגר אשר בשעריך כל הראויה לגר קרויה נבילה שאין ראויה לגר אינה קרויה נבלה

Avodah Zarah 68a:1.english: The Gemara asks: And what is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon? It is as it is taught in a baraita that from the verse: “You shall not eat of any unslaughtered animal carcass; you may give it to the resident alien [la’ger] who is within your gates, that he may eat it” (Deuteronomy 14:21), it is derived that with regard to animal carcasses, anything that is fit for a ger toshav to consume is called an unslaughtered carcass and is forbidden, and any carcass that is unfit even for a ger toshav to consume, e.g., one that turned rancid and is unfit for consumption, is not called an unslaughtered carcass with regard to its prohibition.

Avodah Zarah 68a:12.english: The Gemara suggests another source for the statement of Rabbi Yoḥanan: Come and hear that which is taught in a baraita: In the case of teruma leaven and non-sacred leaven that fell into the dough, if this one was sufficient to cause the dough to become leavened and that one was sufficient to cause the dough to become leavened, and they both cause the dough to become leavened, it is forbidden. Rabbi Shimon deems it permitted. If the teruma leaven fell in first, everyone agrees that it is forbidden. If the non-sacred leaven fell in first and subsequently the teruma leaven or kilayim leaven that were planted in a vineyard fell in, this is also forbidden; but Rabbi Shimon deems it permitted.

Avodah Zarah 68a:9.english: Rav Amram went out, examined the Mishna, and discovered that this dispute is taught in a mishna (Orla 2:8): In the case of non-sacred leaven that fell into the dough, and there is enough of it to cause the dough to become leavened, and the dough indeed became leavened, and subsequently teruma leaven, or kilayim leaven of forbidden planted in a vineyard, fell into this dough, and there is enough of it to cause the dough to become leavened, the dough is forbidden, because the forbidden leaven is considered to have contributed to the process of the leavening. But Rabbi Shimon deems the dough permitted, because the additional leaven has a negative impact on the dough, which was already leavened.

Avodah Zarah 68b:10.english: The Gemara comments: This is as we learned in a mishna (Me’ila 18a): If orla and kilayim planted in a vineyard fell into a permitted substance, and neither one is sufficient in its own quantity to render the mixture forbidden, they combine to render it forbidden if together they are of a sufficient quantity. Rabbi Shimon says: They do not combine, and each forbidden substance is treated individually. Here too, since when the forbidden leaven enhanced the dough, it was not sufficient to enhance it by itself, the permitted leaven does not combine with it to render the dough forbidden.

Avodah Zarah 68b:2.english: And if you would say: Here too, it can be explained as Ulla responded to Rabbi Ḥagga, that the baraita is referring to a case when the vinegar enhanced the flavor of the split beans and subsequently detracted from it, e.g., where it spilled into cold split beans and then they were heated, this cannot be said, as do they actually disagree in a case when the forbidden substance enhanced the flavor of the permitted food and subsequently detracted from it? But isn’t it taught in the first clause of the baraita that if the teruma leaven fell in first, before the non-sacred leaven, everyone agrees that it renders the dough forbidden, as it enhanced the flavor of the dough at the outset, even though the flavor was subsequently detracted from by the non-sacred leaven?

Avodah Zarah 68b:4.english: The Gemara asks: With regard to those three clauses that the baraita teaches concerning different cases, why do I need all three of them? Granted, the last clause, concerning the wine spilling into the lentils, teaches us that the dispute is with regard to a case where the forbidden substance detracts from the flavor of the food from the outset. The middle clause, with regard to the case where the teruma leaven fell in first, also teaches a novel halakha, which is that in the case of a forbidden substance that enhanced the flavor of the food and subsequently detracted from it, everyone agrees that the mixture is forbidden.

Avodah Zarah 68b:5.english: But why do I need the first clause, concerning the case of non-sacred leaven and teruma leaven falling into the dough together? It could have been inferred from the other two clauses that the dough is forbidden, in the following manner: Now that in the case of the last clause, where the forbidden substance does not enhance the permitted food at all, the Rabbis deem it forbidden, is it necessary to say that it is forbidden in the first clause, where the forbidden substance enhances the food’s flavor at first before detracting from it?

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 67b:3:1.hebrew: מדברי כולן נלמד: רב יהודה, ורבה בר בר חנה, ורב דימי, וריש לקיש, ורבי אבהו.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 67b:4:1.hebrew: מכלל דאיכא למאן דאמר וכו': בתמיה: מדאיצטריך רב כהנא למימר "מדברי כולן נלמד", מכלל דאיכא למאן דפליג.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 67b:6:1.hebrew: יליף מגיעולי עובדי כוכבים: דרחמנא אסרינהו בכלי מדין, דכתיב: "כל דבר אשר יבא באש" וגו', דמשמע: הואיל ונשתמש עובד כוכבים בכלי חמין, צריך להרתיח כדי שיפלוט גיעול שבלע.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 67b:6:2.hebrew: לאו נותן טעם לפגם הוא: בתמיה: דהא פשיטא לן, כל תבשיל שלן לילה אחד, נפגם טעמו ועובר צורתו.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 67b:7:1.hebrew: בת יומא: שבישל בה עובד כוכבים היום, דלא נפגם.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 67b:7:2.hebrew: ואידך: אי אפשר דלא פגמה פורתא בתבשיל הבא אחריו, ואפ"ה אסר רחמנא.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:10:1.hebrew: והא הכא - דהאי שאור משעה שנפל ביה פגמה, שהרי מחומצת כבר, וקאסר ר"מ:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:10:1.english: But here - this leaven, from the moment it fell into it, detracted from it, as it was already leavened, and Rabbi Meir prohibits.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:11:1.hebrew: וראויה לחמע בה כמה עיסות אחרות - (של תרומה). הלכך, חימוץ דיותר מדאי, אף על פי שפגם הוא לענין אכילה, שבח הוא לענין חימוע עיסות אחרות:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:11:1.english: And it is suitable for leavening several other batches of dough with it - (of *teruma*). Therefore, excessive leavening, even though it is detrimental for eating, is an enhancement for leavening other doughs.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:12:1.hebrew: שאור של תרומה ושל חולין שנפלו - ביחד לתוך העיסה, ויש בכל אחד כדי לחמץ, וחימצוה יותר מדאי לפוגמה:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:12:1.english: *Teruma* leaven and non-sacred leaven that fell - together into the dough, and each has enough to leaven, and they over-leavened it to its detriment.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:12:2.english: Rabbi Shimon permits - because they spoiled it.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:12:3.hebrew: נפל של תרומה תחלה ד"ה אסור - הואיל ומשביחה בתחלה, אף על פי שחזר והועיל לפוגמה כשנפל שאור של חולין אחריו, ושניהם פגמוה, הוי משביח ולבסוף פגם ואסור. ולקמן פריך: אם כן, רישא נמי ר"ש, הרי השביח של תרומה עם של חולין תחלה:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:12:3.english: *Teruma* leaven fell in first, everyone agrees it is forbidden - since it enhanced it at first, even though it subsequently served to detract from it when the non-sacred leaven fell after it, and both detracted from it, it is considered to have enhanced and then detracted, and is forbidden. And later it asks: If so, the first clause also, Rabbi Shimon, surely the *teruma* enhanced it with the non-sacred leaven at first?

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:12:4.english: Non-sacred leaven fell - and leavened it.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:12:5.hebrew: ואחרי כן נפל של תרומה - דהיינו פוגם מעיקרו, אסור, ור"ש מתיר:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:12:5.english: And afterwards *teruma* leaven fell - which is a case of detracting from the outset, it is forbidden, and Rabbi Shimon permits.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:1:1.hebrew: שאינה ראויה לגר: שהסריחה. אלמא מדאפגים, בטל איסורה.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:2:1.hebrew: סרוחה מעיקרא: מוכת שחין מחיים, דהואיל ואיפגמא מקודם שבאה לידי נבלה, לא חל שם נבלה עליה. אבל היכא דאיתסר מעיקרא, תו לא פקע איסור משום פגם.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:3:1.english: Dispute - of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:3:2.english: In a case where it detracts from the outset - from the moment it fell into it.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:4:1.english: But here it is a case where it detracts from the outset and they disagree - as it teaches that it is forbidden according to the Rabbis.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:9:1.hebrew: שאור של חולין שנפל לתוך העיסה וחימצה - כראוי, ואח"כ נפל של תרומה או של כלאי הכרם, אסור:אשמועינן פלוגתא: The first clause is where they fell in together, and it teaches us the dispute.The middle clause - *teruma* leaven fell in first. The last clause: wine that fell into lentils. The middle clause also teaches us that if it enhanced and then detracted, everyone agrees it is forbidden.Non-sacred leaven that fell into the dough and leavened it - as appropriate, and afterwards *teruma* leaven or *kilayim* of the vineyard fell in, it is forbidden.Rabbi Shimon permits - because they spoiled it.But here - this leaven, from the moment it fell into it, detracted from it, as it was already leavened, and Rabbi Meir prohibits.And it is suitable for leavening several other batches of dough with it - (of *teruma*). Therefore, excessive leavening, even though it is detrimental for eating, is an enhancement for leavening other doughs.The Gemara suggests another source for the statement of Rabbi Yoḥanan: Come and hear that which is taught in a baraita: In the case of *teruma* leaven and non-sacred leaven that fell into the dough, if this one was sufficient to cause the dough to become leavened and that one was sufficient to cause the dough to become leavened, and they both cause the dough to become leavened, it is forbidden. Rabbi Shimon deems it permitted. If the *teruma* leaven fell in first, everyone agrees that it is forbidden. If the non-sacred leaven fell in first and subsequently the *teruma* leaven or *kilayim* leaven that were planted in a vineyard fell in, this is also forbidden; but Rabbi Shimon deems it permitted.*Teruma* leaven and non-sacred leaven that fell - together into the dough, and each has enough to leaven, and they over-leavened it to its detriment.Rabbi Shimon permits - because they spoiled it.*Teruma* leaven fell in first, everyone agrees it is forbidden - since it enhanced it at first, even though it subsequently served to detract from it when the non-sacred leaven fell after it, and both detracted from it, it is considered to have enhanced and then detracted, and is forbidden. And later it asks: If so, the first clause also, Rabbi Shimon, surely the *teruma* enhanced it with the non-sacred leaven at first?Non-sacred leaven fell - and leavened it.And afterwards *teruma* leaven fell - which is a case of detracting from the outset, it is forbidden, and Rabbi Shimon permits.The Gemara comments: But here it is a case where the forbidden substance detracted from the flavor of the dough from the outset, and they disagree. And if you would say: Here too,this can be explained in accordance with the explanation of Rabbi Zeira that dough is different because it is enhanced in any event, come and hear a refutation of that explanation from the latter clause of the same baraita: Forbidden wine that fell into lentils or forbidden vinegar that fell into split beans renders the food forbidden. And Rabbi Shimon deems them permitted. And here also, it is a case where the forbidden substance detracted from the flavor of the dough from the outset, and they disagree.In accordance with Rabbi Zeira - that excessive leavening is an enhancement for leavening other doughs.And if you would say: Here too, it can be explained as Ulla responded to Rabbi Ḥagga, that the baraita is referring to a case when the vinegar enhanced the flavor of the split beans and subsequently detracted from it, e.g., where it spilled into cold split beans and then they were heated, this cannot be said, as do they actually disagree in a case when the forbidden substance enhanced the flavor of the permitted food and subsequently detracted from it? But isn’t it taught in the first clause of the baraita that if the *teruma* leaven fell in first, before the non-sacred leaven, everyone agrees that it renders the dough forbidden, as it enhanced the flavor of the dough at the outset, even though the flavor was subsequently detracted from by the non-sacred leaven?And it teaches: *Teruma* leaven fell in first - which is a case of enhancing and then detracting, and Rabbi Shimon agrees to it.Rather, must one not conclude from it that the dispute is with regard to a case where the forbidden substance detracted from the flavor of the food from the outset? The Gemara affirms: Conclude from it that this is so.The Gemara asks: With regard to those three clauses that the baraita teaches concerning different cases, why do I need all three of them? Granted, the last clause, concerning the wine spilling into the lentils, teaches us that the dispute is with regard to a case where the forbidden substance detracted from the flavor of the food from the outset. The middle clause, with regard to the case where the *teruma* leaven fell in first, also teaches a novel halakha, which is that in the case of a forbidden substance that enhanced the flavor of the food and subsequently detracted from it, everyone agrees that the mixture is forbidden.Three clauses - the first clause is where they fell in together, and it teaches us the dispute.The middle clause - *teruma* leaven fell in first. The last clause: wine that fell into lentils. The middle clause also teaches us that if it enhanced and then detracted, everyone agrees it is forbidden.But why do I need the first clause, concerning the case of non-sacred leaven and *teruma* leaven falling into the dough together? It could have been inferred from the other two clauses that the dough is forbidden, in the following manner: Now that in the case of the last clause, where the forbidden substance does not enhance the permitted food at all, the Rabbis deem it forbidden, is it necessary to say that it is forbidden in the first clause, where the forbidden substance enhances the food’s flavor at first before detracting from it?The last clause, where it does not enhance at all - wine in lentils, the Rabbis prohibit.The first clause - that *teruma* leaven enhanced it along with the non-sacred leaven at first, and then both detracted from it, is it necessary?Abaye said: The first clause is necessary to teach that Rabbi Shimon deems it permitted. And this is what the Rabbis said to Rabbi Shimon: This dough was fit to become leavened in two hours if the permitted leaven had fallen into it alone. What caused it to become leavened in one hour? The forbidden leaven. Therefore, the dough is forbidden.It is necessary for Rabbi Shimon - to teach us that Rabbi Shimon permits.What caused it to become leavened in one hour? The forbidden item - and it is found that it enhanced and then detracted, and in that case, you agree to us that it is forbidden.And Rabbi Shimon could respond that when the two types of leaven enhanced the flavor of the dough, they both enhanced it, not only the forbidden leaven; and when they subsequently detracted from it, they both detracted from it. Therefore, it is permitted.Both enhanced - and not the forbidden item alone enhanced.The Gemara asks: Even according to the opinion of Rabbi Shimon, let the permitted leaven and the forbidden leaven combine together and render the dough forbidden, since Rabbi Shimon concedes that if the permitted food was initially enhanced by the forbidden substance it is forbidden.And it should be forbidden - because of enhancing and then detracting, to which Rabbi Shimon agrees.The Gemara responds: Rabbi Shimon conforms to his standard line of reasoning, as he says that even a forbidden substance and another forbidden substance do not combine to render a mixture forbidden. Accordingly, a forbidden substance and a permitted substance certainly do not.The Gemara comments: This is as we learned in a mishna (Me’ila 18a): If *orla* and *kilayim* planted in a vineyard fell into a permitted substance, and neither one is sufficient in its own quantity to render the mixture forbidden, they combine to render it forbidden if together they are of a sufficient quantity. Rabbi Shimon says: They do not combine, and each forbidden substance is treated individually. Here too, since when the forbidden leaven enhanced the dough, it was not sufficient to enhance it by itself, the permitted leaven does not combine with it to render the dough forbidden.*Orla* and *kilayim* of the vineyard combine - if both fell into less than two hundred.The Gemara recounts an incident involving a certain mouse that fell into a barrel of beer. Rav deemed that barrel of beer forbidden. The Sages said before Rav Sheshet: Shall we say that Rav maintains that even in a case where the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is forbidden? Presumably, the mouse imparted flavor to the detriment of the beer.Rav Sheshet said to them: Rav generally maintains that in a case where the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is permitted. But here, in the case of a mouse, it is a novelty that the Torah prohibits the flavor from a mouse at all, as it is repulsive and people distance themselves from consuming it, and even so the Merciful One prohibits it. Therefore, although it imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is still forbidden.The Sages said to Rav Sheshet: If that is so, that the halakha with regard to a mouse is considered a novelty and is therefore understood to be more stringent than the norm, then a dead mouse should impart ritual impurity whether it is moist or dried out. Why did we learn in a mishna (Nidda 54b) that carcasses of creeping animals impart impurity when they are moist but do not impart impurity when they are dried out?Rav Sheshet responded: And according to your reasoning, in which you compare the halakhot of ritual impurity to forbidden foods, then with regard to semen, which is also repulsive, it should impart impurity whether moist or dried out. Why did we learn in a mishna (Nidda 54b) that semen imparts impurity when it is moist but it does not impart impurity when it is dried out?Rather, what have you to say? With regard to the ritual impurity of semen, the Merciful One states: “The flow of seed” (Leviticus 15:16), meaning that the reference is to semen that is fit to fertilize. Here too, with regard to the ritual impurity of a mouse, the verse states: “When they have died” (Leviticus 11:32). The Merciful One states that the carcasses of creeping animals impart impurity only when they are similar to their state at time of their death, i.e., when they are still moist. Therefore, there is no contradiction to the claim that the prohibition against eating a mouse is a novelty and consequently applies even when it detracted from the flavor of the food into which it fell.Rav Shimi of Neharde’a objects to the assumption that a mouse is repulsive: And is it repulsive? But isn’t it served at the table of kings and considered a delicacy? Rav Shimi of Neharde’a said in clarification: This is not difficult. This statement, that a mouse is served as a delicacy, is stated with regard to a field mouse, and that statement, that it is repulsive, is stated with regard to a city mouse.Rava said: The halakha is that if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is permitted. But with regard to a mouse that fell into a barrel of beer, I do not know what the reason was that Rav deemed it forbidden. I do not know whether it was because he maintains that if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture it is forbidden, and if so, the halakha is not in accordance with his opinion, or whether it was because although he maintains that if the forbidden substance imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture it is permitted, a mouse that falls into beer enhances its flavor.A dilemma was raised before the Sages:If a mouse fell into vinegar, what is the halakha? Does it enhance its flavor? Rav Hillel said to Rav Ashi: There was such an incident in the study hall of Rav Kahana, and Rav Kahana deemed the vinegar forbidden. This indicates that it enhances the flavor. Rav Ashi said to him: This is not a proof. That mouse was dismembered, and Rav Kahana deemed the vinegar forbidden due to concern that one might consume a substantive piece of the mouse in the vinegar, which is prohibited regardless of the taste.The Gemara relates: Ravina thought that the quantity of vinegar necessary for nullifying the flavor of the mouse should be calculated at 101 times the volume of the mouse. He said: It should not be rendered worse, i.e., more stringent, than teruma, which is nullified by 101 times its volume in a mixture. This is as we learned in a mishna (Terumot 4:7): Teruma is nullified in a mixture by 101 times its volume of permitted food. Rav Taḥlifa bar Giza said to Ravina: Perhaps this case is similar to spice of teruma in a pot, whose flavor is not nullified even by 101 times its volume of permitted food, as the flavor imparted by spice is exceptionally strong.Rav Aḥai calculated the amount of vinegar necessary to nullify the flavor of the mouse at fifty times its volume. Although forbidden food in a mixture usually requires the presence of sixty times its volume of permitted food to be nullified, vinegar has a sharp enough flavor that it nullifies the mouse with less. Rav Shmuel, son of Rav Ika, calculated the amount of beer necessary for nullifying the mouse at sixty times the volume of the mouse.The Gemara concludes: And the halakha is that this and that, both vinegar and beer, nullify the mouse with sixty times its volume, and so is the ruling for all prohibitions in the Torah.Non-sacred leaven that fell into the dough and leavened it - as appropriate, and afterwards *teruma* leaven or *kilayim* of the vineyard fell in, it is forbidden.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68a:9:2.english: And Rabbi Shimon permits - because it became too leavened and spoiled.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:10:1.english: *Orla* and *kilayim* of the vineyard combine - if both fell into less than two hundred.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:2:1.hebrew: והקתני נפל של תרומה תחלה - דהשביח ולבסוף פגם הוא, ומודי ר"ש בה:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:2:1.english: And it teaches: *Teruma* leaven fell in first - which is a case of enhancing and then detracting, and Rabbi Shimon agrees to it.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:4:1.hebrew: תלתא בבי - רישא היכא דנפלו כאחת, ואשמועינן פלוגתא:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:4:1.english: Three clauses - the first clause is where they fell in together, and it teaches us the dispute.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:4:2.hebrew: מציעתא - נפל של תרומה תחלה. בבא דסיפא: יין שנפל לתוך עדשים. מציעתא נמי אשמעינן דהשביח ולבסוף פגם דברי הכל אסור:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:4:2.english: The middle clause - *teruma* leaven fell in first. The last clause: wine that fell into lentils. The middle clause also teaches us that if it enhanced and then detracted, everyone agrees it is forbidden.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:5:1.hebrew: סיפא דלא משבח כלל - יין בעדשים, אסרי רבנן:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:5:1.english: The last clause, where it does not enhance at all - wine in lentils, the Rabbis prohibit.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:5:2.hebrew: רישא - דתרומה אשבחיה בהדי שאור דחולין ברישא, והדר פגמה תרוייהו, מיבעיא:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:5:2.english: The first clause - that *teruma* leaven enhanced it along with the non-sacred leaven at first, and then both detracted from it, is it necessary?

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:6:1.english: It is necessary for Rabbi Shimon - to teach us that Rabbi Shimon permits.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:6:2.hebrew: מי גרם לה שתחמץ בשעה אחת איסור - ונמצא דהשביחו ולבסוף פגם, ובההיא הא קא מודית לן דאסור:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:6:2.english: What caused it to become leavened in one hour? The forbidden item - and it is found that it enhanced and then detracted, and in that case, you agree to us that it is forbidden.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:7:1.english: Both enhanced - and not the forbidden item alone enhanced.

Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:8:1.hebrew: וליתסר - משום משביח ולבסוף פגם, דמודי ר"ש בה:
Rashi on Avodah Zarah 68b:8:1.english: And it should be forbidden - because of enhancing and then detracting, to which Rabbi Shimon agrees.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 67b:3.english: Rav Kahana says: From the statements of all the amora’im who were cited (Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, Rabbah bar bar Ḥana, Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, and Reish Lakish), we learn that if a forbidden food imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is permitted. Abaye said to him: Granted, from all of them this conclusion is very well. But how can this be concluded from the statement of Reish Lakish? He says only that the Sages said that if a forbidden food imparts flavor to a permitted food to its detriment, the mixture is permitted, and it implies that he is only citing what others said and he himself does not hold accordingly.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 67b:4.english: The Gemara returns to discuss the main point of Rav Kahana’s statement, and asks: Does it imply by inference from his words that there is one who says that if a forbidden food imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, it is forbidden?

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 67b:5.english: And they answer: Yes, and it is taught in a baraita: Both in a case where the forbidden food imparts flavor to the detriment of the mixture, and in a case where it imparts flavor that enhances the mixture, it is forbidden; this is the statement of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Shimon says: If it enhances the flavor it is forbidden, but if it causes it detriment it is permitted. This shows that Rabbi Meir holds this opinion.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 67b:6.english: And they ask: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir? He derives this halakha from the purging of gentiles' vessels, from pots in which gentiles cooked food, for which the Torah required purification for the vessels that Israel plundered from Midian (Numbers 31:22–23). Is it not the case that the purging of gentiles' vessels imparts a detrimental flavor? For the taste of the food in them becomes spoiled over time and only detracts from the food, and nevertheless, the Merciful One prohibited its use. So too, in every case, it is no different, and even a detrimental flavor is forbidden.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 67b:7.english: And the other tanna, Rabbi Shimon, who permits a detrimental flavor, what does he respond to this proof? He explains in accordance with the statement of Rav Huna, son of Rav Ḥiyya; as Rav Huna, son of Rav Ḥiyya, says: The Torah prohibits only a bat yoma pot (meaning a pot in which the forbidden food was cooked on that very day), because the flavor it imparts is not detrimental. And the other tanna, Rabbi Meir, what does he say? Even a bat yoma pot, it is not possible that it does not detract slightly from the food since it was cooked, and nevertheless, the Torah prohibited it.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 67b:8.english: And they ask: And Rabbi Shimon, who holds that imparting a detrimental flavor is permitted, what is his reasoning for his view? As it is taught in a baraita, it is stated: “You shall not eat of any unslaughtered animal carcass; you may give it to the resident alien who is within your gates, that he may eat it” (Deuteronomy 14:21). From here he learns: Anything that is fit for a ger toshav to eat is called an unslaughtered carcass and is forbidden,

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 68a:1.english: That is unfit for a ger toshav, for example, if it spoiled and became rancid and is unfit for consumption — it is not called an unslaughtered carcass with regard to its prohibition.

Steinsaltz on Avodah Zarah 68a:2.english: And Rabbi Meir, what does he respond to this? He holds: That verse comes to exclude meat that was rancid at the outset, meaning that even in its lifetime it was unfit for consumption due to a repulsive defect, and from the beginning it was not forbidden as a neveilah. But that which was forbidden from the beginning remains forbidden even when its taste becomes detrimental. And Rabbi Shimon, what does he respond to this? Meat that was rancid at the outset does not need exclusion from the verse, because it is considered mere dust, and the name neveilah does not apply to it at all.
